title: MCP 2026-07-28 Specification: Stateless Core & Auth Hardening
content:
## Overview

On July 28, 2026, the Model Context Protocol working group published the **2026-07-28 specification** — the most significant revision to MCP since the protocol's November 2024 debut. Its headline change is that the protocol's transport layer becomes **stateless**, and it substantially hardens MCP's OAuth/OIDC authorization story. Claude Code, Claude Desktop, and Claude Cowork are all adopting the new spec.

---

## Why Stateless

Previous MCP versions relied on a stateful handshake: an `initialize` / `initialized` notification exchange followed by a server-issued `Mcp-Session-Id` header that every subsequent request had to carry. That meant a remote MCP server needed sticky sessions, a shared session store, and often deep packet inspection at the load-balancer layer just to route requests to the right backend instance.

The 2026-07-28 spec removes the handshake and the `Mcp-Session-Id` header entirely from the Streamable HTTP transport. Any request can now be answered by any server instance behind an ordinary round-robin load balancer, since no server-side session state is required between calls.

---

## New Capabilities Enabled by Statelessness

- **Multi Round-Trip Requests** — a single logical operation can span several HTTP round trips without needing a session to tie them together.
- **Header-based routing** — servers can route on an `Mcp-Method` header instead of session affinity.
- **Cacheable list results** — `tools/list` responses can carry a server-specified `ttlMs`, letting clients cache the tool list for that duration instead of re-fetching it on every connection.

---

## Authorization Hardening

Six Specification Enhancement Proposals (SEPs) bring MCP's authorization model in line with real-world OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect deployments. Notable ones:

- **SEP-2468** — clients must validate the `iss` parameter on every authorization response per RFC 9207, mitigating "mix-up" attacks where one authorization server's response is replayed against another.
- **SEP-837** — MCP clients must declare an OpenID Connect `application_type` during Dynamic Client Registration; most OIDC providers reject DCR requests without it, and the previous spec left the field empty.
- **SEP-2352** — clients should use separate credentials per authorization server they interact with, rather than reusing one credential across multiple servers.

The **Enterprise-Managed Authorization** extension also reached stable status in this release. It lets organizations centrally manage authorization for all their MCP servers, so an end user logs in once and gets access to every connected server rather than authenticating separately with each. Anthropic, Microsoft, and Okta are among the early adopters, alongside a growing number of independent MCP servers.

---

## Adoption

Across the Tier 1 SDKs (TypeScript and Python), MCP now sees close to half a billion downloads a month, and both SDKs have individually crossed 1 billion total downloads — a sign of how quickly MCP became the default tool-connection layer for AI agents in under two years.

---

## What This Means for Server Authors

Servers built against the older stateful transport need migration work: session-based auth flows, sticky-session infrastructure, and any code that reads the now-removed `Mcp-Session-Id` header will need to be reworked against the updated Tier 1 SDKs. The spec change is a breaking one for stateful server implementations, though clients that only used the basic request/response flow are largely unaffected.

For teams building MCP servers referenced elsewhere in this wiki (see *Tool Use & Agents*), the practical upshot is that new servers should target the 2026-07-28 spec's stateless model from the start, and existing servers should plan a migration rather than staying pinned to the pre-2026-07-28 transport indefinitely.
